In transamidase, decarboxylase, and deaminase reactions, the 4-formyl (aldehyde) substituent of PLP condenses with the a-amino
group of amino acids substrates to form an azomethine (Schiff-base) linkage. The Schiff-base linkage allows the conjugated double-
bond system to extend into PLP’s pyridinium nitrogen, which weakens bonding around the a-carbon of the amino acid substrate.
Then, depending on the enzyme, transaminations, decarboxylations, or subsequent substitutions at the carbon adjacent to the a-carbon
are facilitated. Stated differently, PLP helps stabilize a carbanion at the a-carbon of the targeted amino acid. Moreover, in PLP-dependent
enzymes, PLP is attached to the ε-amino group of the lysyl group at the active site within the enzyme. This can set the stage for an initial
“transimidation” with an amino acid, which occurs faster than an aldehyde with an amino acid, i.e., transaminations.
In glycogen phosphorylase reactions, the organic ring of PLP functions as a reversible electron sink with the phosphate group of
PLP acting as an acid-base catalyst to prime free phosphate ion for an attack on the terminal glycosidic bond of the glycogen
